strings.name: Svante Pääbo
strings.role: Geneticist · Pioneer of ancient human DNA research
strings.summary: Svante Pääbo is a Swedish geneticist who has long studied ancient DNA in Germany. With interdisciplinary teams, he improved methods for recovering and analysing genetic material from ancient remains, helping reconstruct the Neanderthal genome, identify Denisovans and reveal gene flow with modern human ancestors. He was the sole recipient of the 2022 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine; the scientific work involved extensive collaboration.
strings.coverageNote: Selected early training, ancient-DNA breakthroughs and a 2026 collaborative paper; appointments checked in November 2026. Individual Nobel recognition and collective scientific contributions are described separately.
strings.influence.rationale: He advanced ancient hominin genome research, using ancient-DNA techniques to reconstruct human evolution and genetic connections among ancient populations.

strings.highlights.highlight-1.title: Reconstructing ancient genetic connections
strings.highlights.highlight-1.text: With teams, sequenced the Neanderthal genome and identified Denisovans, revealing interbreeding with ancestors of modern humans.
strings.highlights.highlight-2.title: 2022 Nobel Prize
strings.highlights.highlight-2.text: Sole recipient of the medicine prize for discoveries concerning extinct hominin genomes and human evolution.
strings.timeline.event-1.title: Continues collaborative late-Neanderthal research
strings.timeline.event-1.text: Coauthored work on genetic diversity among late Neanderthals in northwestern Europe, analysing ancient DNA and population relationships with multiple institutions.
strings.timeline.event-2.title: Awarded Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine
strings.timeline.event-2.text: The Nobel Assembly named him the year's sole laureate; the discoveries rested on long-running teams and international collaboration.
strings.timeline.event-3.title: Publishes two ancient-genome breakthroughs
strings.timeline.event-3.text: Teams reported a draft Neanderthal genome and genetic evidence for Denisovans, changing understanding of interactions among ancient hominins.
strings.timeline.event-4.title: Neanderthal DNA and Leipzig research
strings.timeline.event-4.text: His team reported Neanderthal mitochondrial DNA; he also became a founding director of the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Leipzig.
strings.timeline.event-5.title: Becomes professor in Munich
strings.timeline.event-5.text: After postdoctoral work in Zurich and Berkeley, became a professor at the University of Munich, developing ancient genetic research.
strings.timeline.event-6.title: Earns Uppsala doctorate
strings.timeline.event-6.text: Completed doctoral work in cell biology and immunity, then pursued postdoctoral training abroad and expanded his ancient-DNA research.
strings.timeline.event-7.title: Publishes mummy DNA research
strings.timeline.event-7.text: While a doctoral student, published work recovering DNA from an Egyptian mummy, then continued tackling contamination and degradation in ancient DNA.
strings.timeline.event-8.title: Born in Stockholm
strings.timeline.event-8.text: Born in Stockholm, Sweden; later studied humanities and medicine at Uppsala before moving into molecular research.
